source.title: Brownian models of multiclass queueing networks: Current status and open problems

accepted.question_text: For an open queueing network operated under first-in-first-out service at every station, consider the class of networks that are both multiclass and have feedback routing, meaning customers may belong to multiple classes and may revisit stations according to non-feedforward routes. Does there exist a mathematically well-defined approximating Brownian model for this most complex routing class, and can such a model be rigorously justified by heavy-traffic limit theory in the same way as the simpler single-class or feedforward cases?
accepted.context_brief: Brownian approximation for multiclass feedback FIFO networks

evidence.quote: Given our restriction to FIFO scheduling, it is only in the lower right-hand quadrant of table 1 that problems arise in formulating an approximating Brownian model. That is, a rigorous heavy traffic limit theory already exists for all but the most complex routing structures, and that theory supports or justifies the QNET approximation scheme advanced in [11]. Major questions remain unanswered in the lower right-hand quadrant, however,

accepted.question_text: Let d be the number of stations, let G be the d x d routing-information matrix, let theta be the vector of netflow rates, and let Gamma be the covariance matrix in the Brownian approximation. If xi-star is a d-dimensional Brownian motion with drift minus theta and covariance Gamma, does there exist a unique nonnegative process W-star together with a continuous, nondecreasing regulator Y-star such that W-star(t) = xi-star(t) - G W-star(t) + Y-star(t) for all t, with each coordinate Y-star_j allowed to increase only when the corresponding coordinate W-star_j is zero?
accepted.context_brief: Existence and uniqueness of the reduced Brownian system model

evidence.quote: The question remains as to whether for general (θ, Γ, G) there exists a process W* that satisfies (4.24)-(4.28) and whether this process is unique. Although there are partial answers to this question, no definitive account has been given for this problem. This issue must be resolved in order for the Brownian approximation to be fully "justified",

accepted.question_text: For multiclass open queueing networks whose data make the standard Brownian system model ill-defined, what is the correct heavy-traffic limiting framework? In particular, what weaker notion of convergence and what more general class of limit processes, possibly including discontinuous processes, should replace the usual weak convergence to a continuous reflected Brownian model in order to complete the heavy-traffic analysis of such networks?
accepted.context_brief: Generalized heavy-traffic limits beyond the standard Brownian model

evidence.quote: Whitt goes on to describe a larger set of "legitimate" limit processes (which involves more general notions of functions) and a corresponding (weaker) topology from which he is able to establish convergence to a nondegenerate (but oddly behaved) limit process.

Whitt's example together with that of Dai and Wang provide compelling evidence that a more general notion of convergence may be needed in order to complete the treatment of heavy traffic analysis of multiclass open networks. Specifically, a weaker notion of convergence and a more general class of limit processes (e.g. discontinuous processes) may be appropriate for networks whose data result in an ill-defined Brownian system model.
